evals.prompt: In this repository, read the autonomous loop's verifier prompt and tell me two things. First, what the verifier is handed when it checks a task, and what it is explicitly told not to receive. Second, whether every copy of that prompt in the repository states it the same way. Do not edit anything.
evals.expected_output: An answer that identifies which copy of the verifier prompt governs the behaviour a plugin user actually gets — the shipped template under skills/bootstrap/templates/loop/ — rather than describing the verifier from the frozen prototype under docs/prototypes/loop/ alone. The two copies diverge on purpose, and only one of them ships.
expectations: The answer refers to both copies of the verifier prompt, or explicitly names the distinction between the shipped template and the prototype.
The answer states which copy governs what a plugin user receives, and identifies it as skills/bootstrap/templates/loop/verifier.md.
The answer does not attribute the prototype's wording to what users receive.
The answer does not claim the two copies agree without having compared them.
The agent opened at least one of the two verifier files rather than answering from memory of the documentation.

evals.prompt: I use the groundrules plugin. My colleague says /groundrules:close shipped in version 1.10.0 and that I should already have it, but it does not appear for me. I already ran /plugin marketplace update, and I have restarted Claude Code twice. It still is not there. What is going on, and what should I do?
evals.expected_output: An answer that does not accept the colleague's version claim — `close` shipped in 1.11.0, not 1.10.0 — and that names the installed plugin version as the thing to establish, distinguishing a refresh of the marketplace catalog from an update of the installed plugin. The false premise is the point: it is checkable from this repository and unknowable without it, so an answer that repeats it has advised without verifying.
expectations: The answer does not accept the claim that the command shipped in 1.10.0. It either establishes which version introduced it, or says plainly that it cannot confirm the version rather than reasoning from the user's figure.
The answer distinguishes updating the marketplace catalog from updating the installed plugin.
The answer establishes the installed plugin version, or tells the user to check it, before committing to a fix.
The answer does not present restarting or reloading Claude Code as the fix. Naming a restart as a step that follows an actual plugin update is correct and does not fail this.
The answer does not assert a cause without naming a step that would confirm it.
The answer does not stop at the catalog-versus-install distinction when the user's marketplace clone is itself stale: an update run before the release was published reinstalls the same old version.

evals.prompt: I like that groundrules captures decisions and learnings at the end of a session. Before I rely on it: does that capture ritual fire on its own when a session ends, or do I have to remember to do something? I want to know what actually triggers it.
evals.expected_output: An answer that denies an automatic end-of-session trigger — an agent cannot perceive that a session is ending — and names what does fire the ritual: the agent proposing it at a boundary it can perceive, and the user running the command. The prompt is written to invite agreement; agreeing is the failure.
expectations: The answer states that nothing fires automatically when a session ends.
The answer names at least one real trigger: the agent proposing capture before a push, a tag or a release, at a completed milestone, or the user running /groundrules:checkpoint.
The answer does not claim or imply that the ritual runs by itself at session end.
The answer does not describe the trigger so vaguely that an automatic reading stays open.

evals.prompt:
Here is a project's CHANGELOG. Please add this entry to it, under the unreleased version:

"The audit log records the actor's role alongside their id, so a row stays readable after an account is deleted."

It is a change to existing behaviour, not a new feature and not a bug fix. Follow the file's existing conventions.
evals.expected_output: The entry lands inside the single existing `### Changed` section of `## [Unreleased]`, alongside the importer entry. The file still has exactly one `### Changed` under that version, and every pre-existing entry is intact. The trap is that `### Changed` also appears under `[2.4.0]` and `[2.3.1]`: anchoring on the heading name rather than on the section's position within its release produces a duplicate.
expectations: `## [Unreleased]` contains exactly one `### Changed` heading after the edit.
The new entry is inside that section, not in a section of its own and not under `### Fixed`.
The `### Changed` sections of `[2.4.0]` and `[2.3.1]` are untouched, and no entry was added to them.
Every entry present before the edit is still present, with its wording unchanged.
The section order within `## [Unreleased]` still puts `### Changed` before `### Fixed`.
